Author persona (Inge Salas): d.procedure is realized where it carries feeling rather than information, Graciela synchronizing the clocks, logging four tenths of a second and feeling better; d.delay in the sleep-and-tea exchange and the crossed start-tonight and closing-me lines, with literal content clear; d.scale once, the lentil of sunlight that is the whole Sun. d.anomaly is correctly unused before the discovery. Weakness: the narration twice names a feeling outright (\"found she was grateful\", \"felt better\") where a gesture could carry it; \"smaller than her handwriting\" is close to too clever. Smallest repair: none now; in scene 2 let the discovery show through actions. Graciela: engineering exactness and dry short replies (\"Either.\", \"That is my name.\", \"So did I.\") follow from her modeled control of timing and composed-reply latency; her tenderness appears only as noticing (the one chair, the tape), which fits a mother share of 0.44 held under work. Risk: every line is short, which would flatten her by scene 3; she needs one longer unguarded speech there. Candelaria, seen from outside: stacked questions, the unasked-for tea, the self-correction from Chela, and exact numbers about the map; warmer and more awkward than her daughter, consistent with 26 hours a month of careful letters and no practice at replies. Her interiority is deliberately deferred to scene 2.","data":{"reviewedGraphHash":"9e8e4e44180e77ce11f6b3215ddeafaf4d8c07be21caf15cd4b5f8135c8a21e8","modelHash":"2d857b5f5fa989ec6b7b4d74f0a80743741d4fe47b46731e437f4e0a3c5ff4fb","authorModelNodeId":"author-model","subjects":{"author":{"dispositions":["d.procedure","d.delay","d.scale"],"weakness":"named feelings twice","repair":"none now; actions in scene 2"},"referent.engineer":{"evidence":["life-trends#tr.control","life-trends#tr.latency","/processes cut.engineer.d00.attention.v2"],"risk":"all lines short","repair":"one longer unguarded speech in scene 3"},"referent.astronomer":{"evidence":["life-trends#tr.contact","life-trends#tr.keeps"],"note":"interiority deferred to scene 2"}}},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":47}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"draft","text":"* * *

On the eighth day Candelaria woke at three, as she had woken at three for eleven years, and found the console light already on.

Her daughter was asleep on the crate with her back against the module frame and a data cable looped twice around her wrist, the way you tie up a boat. For a week she had slept like that, in pieces, between calibrations. She ate standing. She said "copy" instead of "yes". Candelaria had catalogued these things the way she catalogued anything that arrived at the station, carefully and without conclusions, and she had not yet found the question they answered.

At 03:40 La Mancha came round into the window, and the pipeline woke, and so did Graciela, all at once, the cable already in her other hand.

The first live difference map took eleven minutes. Most of it was nothing: a grey field of noise, which is what an unchanged world looks like when you subtract it from itself. Across La Mancha there were stripes.

They were faint and parallel and evenly spaced, a dozen of them, and the fault detector drew a box around them and wrote CALIBRATION FAULT — ALIGNMENT, T07? in the yellow the agency kept for things you could fix.

"Mierda," Graciela said quietly. "That's mine." She was already pulling telescope seven's alignment logs. "Seven's been drifting since the approach. I thought I'd trimmed it."

Candelaria looked at the stripes. She had looked at La Mancha for eleven years and it had never had stripes, and she felt, for a moment, the particular embarrassment of an old instrument caught out by a new one.

"They stop at the coast," she said.

Graciela did not look up. "What?"

"They stop where the mat stops. An alignment fault would stripe the whole frame."

Graciela looked. She was quiet for a while, the logs still scrolling under her hand.

"Run it on the last window," Candelaria said.

"The pipeline wasn't calibrated a week ago."

"The raw data is there. Every window since '20 is there." She heard her voice come out in the tone she kept for the agency, and did not stop it. "If we ask Earth, the answer comes back after the next window has gone. One orbit is six days; a question and its answer take nearly eight. Nobody can steer this from there."

Her daughter looked at her then, properly, for perhaps the first time that week. Then she turned back to the console and began to set up the run.

It took most of the night. The pipeline reprojected both windows, the one from a week ago and the one from tonight, out of the instrument's frame and onto the ground, onto the planet's own latitude and longitude, as if the twelve telescopes had never existed. Graciela fitted the edges of the stripes against the static model to a fraction of a pixel, because that was how she did everything.

At 06:12 the two maps lay over each other on the screen, and the stripes were in the same places on the ground. Not on the detector. On the ground. And the bright edge of each one had moved east by the same distance, 3.1 kilometres, in one orbit.

"An artifact lives in the instrument's frame," Candelaria said. Her mouth was dry. "This lives in theirs."

"Whose?" Graciela said.

Neither of them answered.

Graciela put both hands flat on the console, as if it might move, and laughed once, a short surprised sound Candelaria had last heard from her at eight, when a kite went up on the first try.

Then the arithmetic came, because it always came: swaths eight kilometres wide, growing back, by the brightness of the fresh edges, in something like a hundred and ninety days, and moving on across nine hundred kilometres. In eleven years every part of La Mancha had been cut and had grown back many times, and the average of all of it was the even dark on her map; her own change checks, built for clouds at forty kilometres a pixel, would never have seen a single swath.

She had integrated it away. Eleven years of patience, the thing she was best at, and what it had kept for her so faithfully was the average. The field had never once held still.

She found that she was standing in the galley with the kettle in her hand, and did not remember going there. She thought about the ones who cut. She thought about light that had left forty years ago, about whatever had done this before anyone at the agency was born, which might have stopped since or might be doing it tonight, in a present she would never see. She thought about 2220, her first month here, and how she had decided then that the field was quiet. She did not, she noticed later, think about her daughter at all.

She wrote the report the next day, the way she wrote everything that had to cross ninety-three hours: slowly, and more than once. *Linear parallel features in La Mancha, about eight kilometres wide, advancing east at 3.1 km per orbit in the planet-fixed frame; instrument origin excluded by reprojection across two windows. Interpretation: consistent with cultivation by an agent. A grazing front or a die-back front is not excluded.* She took out *consistent with* and put it back. She took out *by an agent* and put it back. She thought of a committee on Earth reading it in four days, and wrote it plainer.

At 14:20 on the tenth day she sent it, and it began its ninety-three hours. Any answer would reach the station on the eighteenth day. The *Starling* left on the sixteenth.

When she looked up the console module was empty. The crate had its cushion and its cord and no one on it. On the comms panel the *Starling*'s crew channel showed a message being composed, outbound, to Earth, a long one; the counter said it had been open for an hour and twelve minutes.

She had not heard her daughter leave.","data":{"scene":"scene-2","passages":["s2-p1","s2-p2","s2-p3","s2-p4","s2-p5","s2-p6"]},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":49}}

upsertNodes.text:
She wrote the report the next day, the way she wrote everything that had to cross ninety-three hours: slowly, and more than once. *Linear parallel features in La Mancha, about eight kilometres wide, advancing east at 3.1 km per orbit in the planet-fixed frame; instrument origin excluded by reprojection across two windows. Interpretation: consistent with cultivation by an agent. A grazing front or a die-back front is not excluded.* She took out *consistent with* and put it back. She took out *by an agent* and put it back. She thought of a committee on Earth reading it in four days, and wrote it plainer.

At 14:20 on the tenth day she sent it, and it began its ninety-three hours. Any answer would reach the station on the eighteenth day. The *Starling* would leave on the sixteenth.

When she looked up the console module was empty. The crate had its cushion and its cord and no one on it. On the comms panel the *Starling*'s crew channel showed a message being composed, outbound, to Earth, a long one; the counter said it had been open for an hour and twelve minutes.

She had not heard her daughter leave.

upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Voice review of scene 2 (self-review). Author persona: d.anomaly is the scene's engine, a yellow fault box doubted before it is believed, wonder shown as a laugh and a kettle she does not remember picking up; d.procedure makes belief procedural (reprojection, edge fitting); d.scale once, forty-year-old light against a present she will never see. Weakness: the arithmetic paragraph is dense and at the exposition limit; \"She had integrated it away\" states the insight outright. Kept deliberately: it is the one sentence the story most needs said plainly, and the next sentence turns it on her. Candelaria, now from inside: she catalogues without conclusions (the cable, copy instead of yes) and speaks in instrument language that turns personal (\"This lives in theirs\"), consistent with her waiting horizon and reliance on keeping; the scatter of her attention is shown and the omission of her daughter is noticed only afterwards, as the day-9 Cut (daughter 0.18) implies. Risk: she is articulate because this is her domain; in scene 3 she must be less fluent. Graciela from outside: she claims the fault as hers (\"That is mine\") out of competence and control, asks the single question that opens the cultivators (\"Whose?\"), and the laugh from the kite at eight is the one unguarded thing in the scene; the long outbound message fits her home share rising to 0.27 and her composed replies. Smallest repair: none; carry the fluency risk into scene 3.","data":{"modelHash":"2d857b5f5fa989ec6b7b4d74f0a80743741d4fe47b46731e437f4e0a3c5ff4fb","authorModelNodeId":"author-model","subjects":{"author":["d.anomaly","d.procedure","d.scale"],"referent.astronomer":["life-trends#tr.keeps","life-trends#tr.waiting","cut.astronomer.d09.attention.v2"],"referent.engineer":["life-trends#tr.control","cut.engineer.d09.attention.v2"]}},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":54}}

upsertNodes.text: On day 15, before telling each other, Candelaria and then Graciela separately tell Kaya, the Starling's pilot, that they are not boarding. Each means the other to go home: Candelaria stays and would send her daughter home to Tomas; Graciela would stay in her mother's place, as the human the decision loop needs, and send her mother home after eleven years.

upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"context","text":"Story plan revision 2 (supersedes plan for scene 3; scenes 1 and 2 are committed as planned, with the fixes recorded in their audit assessments). Scene 3, Deadline (day 15 to 16), viewpoint Graciela, reader order 3. The day-14 window confirmed the advance a third time. Each woman has separately told Kaya, the Starling's pilot, that she is not boarding, and each meant it to send the other home: Candelaria arranged astronomer_stays (she stays; her daughter goes home to Tomas), believing as always that her daughter will keep; Graciela arranged engineer_stays (she stays in her mother's place as the human the decision loop needs; her mother goes home after eleven years), using the timing habit she learned from her mother's extensions. Kaya tells Graciela her mother gave the same speech an hour earlier. The confrontation: Candelaria asks her to go home and promises to write; Graciela answers in one longer unguarded speech that uses the discovery against her mother's belief: things do not keep, only their averages do. Neither will leave the other at 672 AU; the stores make two residents a two-year bet on an early ship that Earth cannot confirm before day 16. Graciela writes to Tomas; her instinct is to send it after the Starling has gone, when it can no longer be undone; her mother tells her to send it now, while she could still change her mind, and she does. The Starling leaves as a moving point with Kaya and Brandt. Final beat: planning the next window (day 20), Graciela answers her mother's question before it is finished. The drawn remainder is therefore the collision of two attempted named continuations (friction note G14), and it must read as their choice, with each woman's reason visible.","data":{"supersedes":"plan","scene3":{"worldTime":15,"worldTimeEnd":16.01,"viewpoint":"referent.engineer","readerOrder":3}},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":58}}

upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"context","text":"Story plan revision 3 (supersedes plan-2 in one respect; everything else in plan-2 stands). Candelaria's motive for arranging her daughter's return is corrected against the model: by day 15 her reliance has moved from the average (0.15) to the person (0.33), with 0.25 unresolved, so she does not send Graciela home believing she will keep. She sends her home because she has just learned that nothing keeps: Tomas's waiting will not keep either, and a person is kept only by attention. For herself the old reliance survives (record 0.17): she offers to write. The scene should show both at once, the lesson applied to her daughter and not yet to herself, and Graciela's long speech turns the lesson back on her.","authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":59}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"draft","text":"* * *

The window on the fourteenth came in at 18:05, and the edges had moved again: 3.1 kilometres, the same as before, as if whoever was doing it kept a calendar. Three windows now, one orbit apart, agreeing. Graciela ran the reprojection twice and logged it and did not tell her mother that she had run it twice.

On the fifteenth she crossed to the *Starling* at six in the morning, before her mother was up, and found Kaya in the cockpit doing the departure checklist with a bulb of coffee held in his teeth.

"I'm not coming," she said. "I'll sign whatever the agency needs. The station needs someone in the loop; you've heard her, a question to Earth takes longer than an orbit. My mother's done eleven years. She goes home. I stay."

Kaya took the coffee out of his mouth. He looked at her for a long moment with an expression she could not read, and then he began, very quietly, to laugh.

"What."

"Your mother," Kaya said, "was here an hour ago. Same speech. Different names." He wiped his eyes. "She's staying, and you're going home to your Tomás, and she'd take it as a kindness if I didn't let you argue."

Graciela stood in the cockpit door with her hand on the frame. She thought, with great clarity, of every message she had ever timed. She thought of her mother at five in the morning in this same doorway, choosing her words the way she chose them for the agency, and doing it first, so that by the time Graciela knew, it would already be arranged.

"She timed it," she said.

"You both did." Kaya put the coffee back in his teeth. "I leave at noon tomorrow. You two work out which of you I'm taking. Or neither," he added. "But I'd like to know by dinner."

Her mother was in the galley, in the one chair, with two mugs on the counter. She had not drunk from either.

"Kaya told you," she said.

"Kaya told me."

"Chela—" Her mother stopped, and this time did not correct it. "Tomás said two years. You told me that the first night. Two years is— he's waiting now, today. That doesn't keep. I know that now. I didn't know it a week ago." She turned one of the mugs a quarter turn. "You go home. I'll write. I'll write every day, I've had the practice."

It was the most she had said at once since the arrival, and none of it was in order, and Graciela understood that her mother had not rehearsed it, or had rehearsed it and lost the order on the way.

"You'll write," Graciela said. And then, because there were no ninety-three hours to hide in, and no one to arrange it for her, she said the rest.

"You wrote to me every day for eleven years, mamá. Long letters. I have all of them. I used to read them at night and I could hear you composing, I could hear you choosing. And I answered in four lines, four days later, and do you know what I learned? That you could do that. That you could love someone in a way that arrived ninety-three hours late and still call it love, and it was, I'm not saying it wasn't. But you showed me last week what it's worth. Eleven years of looking, and all it kept was the average. The field was being cut the whole time. I was being cut the whole time. You don't get to go back to letters now that you know. And I'm not going home to wait four days for you to answer me. I did that. I did it for eleven years, and I got so good at it that I did it to Tomás."

She had not known she was going to say the last thing until it was said.

Her mother said nothing for a long time. Then she said, "The stores are fourteen hundred and sixty person-days."

"I know what the stores are."

"Two of us is two years. The next ship is four." Her mother's hands were flat on the counter now, the way Graciela's had been on the console. "It's a bet. That they read the report and send a ship early. That they believe it."

"They'll believe it."

"We can't know that before noon tomorrow."

"No," Graciela said. "We can't know anything before noon tomorrow. That's what it's like here. You told me."

Her mother looked at her, and Graciela watched her do the arithmetic, and arrive at the end of it, and not like the answer, and choose it anyway.

"Both, then," her mother said.

"Both."

It was not what either of them had arranged. It was, Graciela thought, the first thing in eleven years they had decided in the same room.

She wrote to Tomás in the console module, on the crate. It took an hour and it was not four lines. When it was done she set the send time for 12:05 tomorrow, five minutes after the *Starling* would be gone, and looked at that for a while.

"Send it now," her mother said from the door.

"He can't answer in time. It gets there after the ship's gone either way."

"That isn't what it's for." Her mother did not come in. "If you send it now, then when he reads it, it will have been true for a whole day that you could still have gone. He should have that."

Graciela thought about a message that had arrived when *don't* was a word about the past. She cleared the send time, and sent it, and it began its ninety-three hours to Valparaíso.

At noon on the sixteenth Kaya and Brandt took the *Starling* off the collar. They watched from the galley port. For a few minutes it was a shape, its drive not yet lit, and then the drive lit and it was a point, and then it was a point that moved, which was the only way to tell it from a star.

Afterwards her mother took the one chair and Graciela took the crate, and they began on the next window, which was four days out. "If we put seven and nine in the near infrared," her mother said, "then the fresh edges should—"

"—separate from the regrowth by the second pass," Graciela said. "I've already queued it."

Her mother looked at her. On the counter between them the Sun lay in its spot the size of a lentil, and neither of them said anything about how long the answer had taken, which was no time at all.","data":{"scene":"scene-3","passages":["s3-p1","s3-p2","s3-p3","s3-p4","s3-p5","s3-p6","s3-p7","s3-p8"]},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":61}}

upsertNodes.text: On day 15 both women decide to stay at the Landing. The Starling will leave on day 16 with its two-person crew and leave behind the rations it carried for them; two residents then have about two years and six weeks of stores.

The station's stores hold 1,460 person-days: one resident for four years, two for about two. The Starling can leave the 80 person-days it carried for two returning passengers, which adds about six weeks for two. The next scheduled relief ship is about four years away.

A dozen swaths, each about 8 km wide and about 75 km from the next, all advance east 3.1 km per orbit, so any one place is cut again about every 148 days, and the mat regrows over a swath in about 145 days: a rotation, not a single front. Over eleven years every part of La Mancha was cut and regrew some twenty-seven times, and the long average is uniform. The station's own change checks were for clouds, at about 40 km per pixel, where 8 km swaths vanish. The 3.1 km shift is measured by fitting each swath edge to a fraction of a 3.8 km pixel against the static model.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-1
upsertNodes.text:
The hatch at the end said FOCAL STATION T1E in agency letters, and under that, on a strip of tape, in a hand she knew better than her own: *the Landing*. It opened before she touched it.

Her mother was smaller than her handwriting. That was the first thing, and it was unfair, and Graciela noticed herself noticing it. Candelaria Araya had been cutting her own hair since 2220, and it stood up grey on one side where the scissors had not reached. She was holding a mug in both hands. She did not put it down.

Neither of them spoke for long enough that it became a decision. Graciela could feel the old habit arriving: the message composed, the message sent, ninety-three hours out and ninety-three back, and between them the long flat time in which nothing was required of you. There was no such time here. Her mother was a metre away, breathing.

"Did you sleep?" her mother said. "On the way. Kaya said the bunks are bad." And then, before Graciela could decide anything: "Do you want tea? I have tea. Real leaves."

"Eleven months, mamá," Graciela said. "I slept."

Her mother nodded as if that answered the tea as well, and it was only later, sitting in the galley with a mug she had not asked for, that Graciela understood she had been given the tea anyway.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-1
upsertNodes.text:
The galley was one person wide. There was one chair, bolted at the counter, and beside it a supply crate with a cushion tied on with cord, and she understood that the crate had been a chair for no one for eleven years and was being a chair for her now. The tea was in a jar labelled in her mother's hand, *2219*. The galley port had its blind down, and through the hole where the blind's cord ran, sunlight lay on the counter in a spot no bigger than a lentil. It was the whole Sun.

"Chela," her mother said, and stopped. "Graciela."

"Either."

"You sign them G. Mardones."

"That's my name."

"It's half your name. The other half is mine." Her mother turned the mug. "I called you Chela until I left. After that I thought I should— you were eighteen."

For eleven years her mother had written to her nearly every day, long careful messages that read like letters, an hour of composing at a time. Graciela had answered, when she answered, days later and in four lines. The messages had begun *Chela* until the year her mother left and *Graciela* ever after, and Graciela had never asked why, because a question took ninety-three hours to arrive and ninety-three to come back, and by then she would have had to mean it.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-1
upsertNodes.text:
On the main screen the coronagraph held the Sun behind a black disc, and around the disc, a hair's breadth out, lay a ring of faint red light. "It's never a picture," her mother said. "Every point on that ring has the whole planet in it." The light in the ring had left TRAPPIST-1e forty years ago, ten years before Graciela was born.

Her mother leaned past her, which put her arm against Graciela's shoulder for the first time since she was eighteen, and brought up the map. The planet kept one face to its red star. On the eastern edge of the day side, where it began to go dark, lay a region the colour of a bruise.

"La Mancha," Graciela said, before her mother could. The stain, and the plain in Spain with the wheat and the windmills; she had been twenty when the joke arrived in a letter, and twenty-six when the letter came that said it was alive. Nine hundred kilometres of something photosynthetic, black across everything a red star gave it.

"Eleven years of light, at three point eight kilometres a pixel," her mother said. "It hasn't changed by one."

Graciela looked at the dark, even texture of it. It looked, she thought, like a very long exposure of nothing happening.

"It's the steadiest thing I know," her mother said.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-2
upsertNodes.text:
* * *

On the eighth day Candelaria woke at three, as she had woken at three for as long as she had lived here, and found the console light already on.

Her daughter was asleep on the crate with her back against the module frame and a data cable looped twice around her wrist, the way you tie up a boat. For a week she had slept like that, in pieces, between calibrations. She ate standing. She said "copy" instead of "yes". Candelaria had catalogued these things the way she catalogued anything that arrived at the station, carefully and without conclusions, and she had not yet found the question they answered.

At 03:40 La Mancha came round into the window, and the pipeline woke, and so did Graciela, all at once, the cable already in her other hand.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-2
upsertNodes.text:
The first live difference map took eleven minutes. Most of it was nothing: a grey field of noise, which is what an unchanged world looks like when you subtract it from itself. Across La Mancha there were stripes.

They were faint and parallel and evenly spaced, a dozen of them, and the fault detector drew a box around them and wrote CALIBRATION FAULT — ALIGNMENT, T07? in the yellow the agency kept for things you could fix.

"Mierda," Graciela said quietly. "That's mine." She was already pulling telescope seven's alignment logs. "Seven's been drifting since the approach. I thought I'd trimmed it."

Candelaria looked at the stripes. She had looked at La Mancha for a decade and it had never had stripes, and she felt, for a moment, the particular embarrassment of an old instrument caught out by a new one.

"They stop at the coast," she said.

Graciela did not look up. "What?"

"They stop where the mat stops. An alignment fault would stripe the whole frame."

upsertNodes.subject: scene-2
upsertNodes.text:
Then the arithmetic came, because it always came. A dozen swaths, eight kilometres wide and seventy-five apart, were moving east together, so any one place was cut again every five months, just as it had grown back; in the years she had been watching, every part of La Mancha had been cut twenty-seven times. Her change checks had been built for clouds, at forty kilometres a pixel, where an eight-kilometre swath is not there at all.

She had integrated it away. The patience she was best at had kept for her, faithfully, the average of all that cutting: the even dark on her map. The field had never once held still.

She found that she was standing in the galley with the kettle in her hand, and did not remember going there. She thought about the ones who cut. She thought about light that had left forty years ago, about whatever had done this before her daughter was born, which might have stopped since or might be doing it tonight, in a present she would never see. She thought about 2220, her first month here, and how she had decided then that the field was quiet. She did not, she noticed later, think about her daughter at all.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
* * *

The window on the fourteenth came in at 06:05, and the edges had moved again: 3.1 kilometres, the same as before, as if whoever was doing it kept a calendar. Three windows now, one orbit apart, agreeing. Graciela ran the reprojection twice and logged it and did not tell her mother that she had run it twice.

On the fifteenth she crossed to the *Starling* at six in the morning, before her mother was up, and found Kaya in the cockpit doing the departure checklist with a bulb of coffee held in his teeth.

"I'm not coming," she said. "I'll sign whatever the agency needs. The station needs someone in the loop; you've heard her, a question to Earth takes longer than an orbit. My mother's done eleven years. She goes home. I stay."

Kaya took the coffee out of his mouth. He looked at her for a long moment with an expression she could not read, and then he began, very quietly, to laugh.

"What."

"Your mother," Kaya said, "was here an hour ago. Same speech. Different names." He wiped his eyes. "She's staying, and you're going home to your Tomás, and she'd take it as a kindness if I didn't let you argue."

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
"You'll write," Graciela said. And then, because there were no ninety-three hours to hide in, and no one to arrange it for her, she said the rest.

"You wrote to me every day, mamá. I have all of them. I used to read them at night and I could hear you choosing the words. And I answered in four lines, four days later, and do you know what I learned from that? That you can love someone ninety-three hours late and still call it love. I'm not going home to wait for your letters. I got so good at waiting that I did it to Tomás."

She had not known she was going to say the last thing until it was said.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
Her mother said nothing for a long time. Then she said, "The stores are fourteen hundred and sixty person-days."

"I know what the stores are."

"Two of us is two years. The next ship is four."

"Kaya can leave what he brought for us going home," Graciela said. "Eighty days."

"Six weeks, for two." Her mother did the division without looking up. Her mother's hands were flat on the counter now, the way Graciela's had been on the console. "It's a bet. That they read the report and send a ship early. That they believe it."

"They'll believe it."

"We can't know that before noon tomorrow."

"No," Graciela said. "We can't know anything before noon tomorrow. That's what it's like here. You told me."

Graciela thought of her mother alone here for four more years, sixty-two, with the only thing like it anyone had ever seen and no one to tell in less than four days.

Her mother looked at her, and Graciela watched her do the arithmetic, and arrive at the end of it, and not like the answer, and choose it anyway.

"Both, then," her mother said.

"Both."

It was not what either of them had arranged. It was, Graciela thought, the first thing since she was eighteen that they had decided in the same room.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
She wrote to Tomás in the console module, on the crate. It took an hour and it was not four lines. It ended with the date of the next ship and one sentence she rewrote six times: *I am asking you to wait, which is the thing I never forgave anyone for asking.* When it was done she set the send time for 12:05 tomorrow, five minutes after the *Starling* would be gone, and looked at that for a while.

"Send it now," her mother said from the door.

"He can't answer in time. It gets there after the ship's gone either way."

"That isn't what it's for." Her mother did not come in. "If you send it now, then when he reads it, it will have been true for a whole day that you could still have gone. He should have that."

Graciela thought about a message that had arrived when *don't* was a word about the past. She cleared the send time, and sent it, and it began its ninety-three hours to Valparaíso.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
Afterwards her mother took the one chair and Graciela took the crate, and they began on the next window, which was four days out. "If we put seven and nine in the near infrared," her mother said, "then the fresh edges should—"

"—separate from the regrowth by the second pass," Graciela said. "I've already queued it."

Her mother looked at her. On the counter between them the Sun lay in its spot the size of a lentil, and neither of them said anything about how long the answer had taken.

The only record change is the audit-prompted correction of canon.announcement (the objection had to reach Graciela aboard the ship, not Earth), which sharpens the record the decision symmetry depends on. Model revision 3 is unchanged, so all earlier model evidence stands.","evidence":[{"kind":"node","nodeId":"canon.announcement"},{"kind":"node","nodeId":"assess-audit-scene-1"},{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/events/12"}],"smallestRepair":null},{"subject":"Scene 3: Candelaria arranges astronomer_stays and asks her daughter to go home","status":"sufficient","explanation":"Her attributed intention (stay, send her daughter home, tell Kaya first) is explained by her decide-first habit (the two extensions), her day-15 attention (daughter 0.49, field 0.25) and, after plan-3, by the lesson of day 9: her reliance has moved to the person (0.33) with 0.25 unresolved, so she sends her daughter home because Tomas's waiting will not keep, while her own reliance on the record (0.17) survives as the offer to write.","evidence":[{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/events/40"},{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/normalized_cuts/6"},{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/normalized_cuts/13"},{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/events/36"},{"kind":"node","nodeId":"plan-3"},{"kind":"node","nodeId":"canon.pilot"}],"smallestRepair":null},{"subject":"Scene 3: Graciela arranges engineer_stays without asking","status":"sufficient","explanation":"Her intention (stay as the human the loop needs, send her mother home) is explained by the decision loop (orbit 6.1 days, round trip 7.77), the confirming day-14 window, her control of timing (6.75), and her belief that her mother would not come home if asked (3.50), which is why she arranges rather than asks. Neither leaves because each will not leave the other alone at 672 AU (day-15 shares daughter 0.49 and mother 0.45), the loop needs someone, and the stores make it a two-year bet on an early ship the report may bring but Earth cannot confirm before day 16.","evidence":[{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/event_relations/56"},{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/event_relations/57"},{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/normalized_cuts/11"},{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/events/32"},{"kind":"model","path":"/processes/12"},{"kind":"node","nodeId":"direction-continuation"}],"smallestRepair":null},{"subject":"Scene 3: the untimed message to Tomas, and the final real-time answer","status":"sufficient","explanation":"Graciela's instinct to send it after the ship has gone follows from her control of timing; her mother's insistence that she send it now comes from having received a timed message herself (the announcement) and from the lesson that a person is kept only by attention. The parting at launch gives the message its cost. The final answer before the question ends is a shown adaptation of her reply-latency trend (108 hours at entry) in the new real-time situation; the dossier leaves her future open, so no model value is contradicted.","evidence":[{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/events/33"},{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/events/34"},{"kind":"model","path":"/processes/9"},{"kind":"node","nodeId":"canon.announcement"},{"kind":"node","nodeId":"canon.tomas"},{"kind":"node","nodeId":"plan-3"}],"smallestRepair":null},{"subject":"Deepening pass 1: the rotation arithmetic and the rations, as revised","status":"sufficient","explanation":"The independent reader showed the concealment arithmetic did not hold as one front. Revision 5 makes it a rotation: twelve swaths 75 km apart advancing 3.1 km per orbit recut each place every ~148 days, regrowth ~145 days, about twenty-seven cycles in eleven years, so the long average is uniform by construction. The Starling's 80 spare person-days close the rations hole and leave the bet in place (about two years and six weeks against a ship four years away). The prose now states the rotation and the six weeks, and Graciela's reason for staying is on the page.","evidence":[{"kind":"model","path":"/processes/20"},{"kind":"model","path":"/processes/21"},{"kind":"model","path":"/processes/22"},{"kind":"model","path":"/processes/18"},{"kind":"model","path":"/processes/23"},{"kind":"model","path":"/meaning_model/events/32"},{"kind":"node","nodeId":"canon.why_missed"},{"kind":"node","nodeId":"canon.stores"},{"kind":"node","nodeId":"independent-reader-1"},{"kind":"node","nodeId":"deepen-1-plan"}],"smallestRepair":null}],"semanticVerification":false},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":77}}

upsertNodes.text: On day 15 both women decide to stay at the Landing. The Starling will leave on day 16 with its two-person crew and leave behind the rations it carried for them; two residents then have nearly three years of stores against a relief ship about four years away.

On day 10 Candelaria sends the agency a hedged report of straight parallel swaths advancing across La Mancha, with the frame test. Before sending it she rules out self-organised banding of the kind tiger bush makes on Earth: the swaths are straight, never fork, and all advance at one rate. The report leaves a grazing front or a die-back front open. It reaches Earth about day 13.9; no reply can arrive before the Starling must leave.

The station's stores hold 1,460 person-days: one resident for four years, two for about two. The Starling carries about 670 person-days for its two returning passengers on the eleven-month voyage home and can leave them, which gives two residents nearly three years in all. The next scheduled relief ship is about four years away.

From 672 AU the Sun is a point about three arcseconds across, about as bright as a full Moon seen from Earth (about a quarter of a lux), and it casts sharp shadows, which show only where the lights are low: the docking tube before its lights come on, and the galley Candelaria keeps dim. With the Sun occulted, TRAPPIST-1e appears as a thin ring of light just outside the Sun's disk, an Einstein ring; every point on the ring carries light from the whole planet, so a map is a reconstruction, never a picture.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-1
upsertNodes.text:
The docking tube was forty metres of ribbed white fabric, and the Sun was in it.

It came through a port halfway along, a point so bright that Graciela put up her hand without thinking, and in the unlit tube her hand threw a shadow on the wall with edges as clean as a cut. She had read that it would be like this: at six hundred and seventy-two astronomical units the Sun was three seconds of arc across, which is to say a point, and about as bright as a full Moon over Valparaíso. Reading it had not prepared her for the shadow. Nothing in eleven months on the *Starling* had cast one.

Behind her Kaya, who with Brandt made up the *Starling*'s entire crew, said, "Sixteen days," the way he had said it every morning of the approach, as if it were a greeting. The return burn was fixed. On the sixteenth day the ship would leave, with the autonomy installed or not, and with the station's resident aboard.

"I know," she said, and pulled herself on.

Through the next port there was nothing to see, which was correct. Twelve one-metre telescopes held formation out there across a patch of dark three kilometres wide, the image plane, where the Sun's gravity brought one planet's light to a focus. They flew with their lights off, so as not to see themselves.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-1
upsertNodes.text:
The galley was one person wide. There was one chair, bolted at the counter, and beside it a supply crate with a cushion tied on with cord, and she understood that the crate had been a chair for no one for eleven years and was being a chair for her now. The tea was in a jar labelled in her mother's hand, *2219*. Her mother kept the galley dim, and the port had its blind down; through the hole where the blind's cord ran, sunlight lay on the counter in a spot no bigger than a lentil. It was the whole Sun.

"Chela," her mother said, and stopped. "Graciela."

"Either."

"You sign them G. Mardones."

"That's my name."

"It's half your name. The other half is mine." Her mother turned the mug. "I called you Chela until I left. After that I thought I should— you were eighteen."

For eleven years her mother had written to her nearly every day, long careful messages that read like letters, an hour of composing at a time. Graciela had answered, when she answered, days later and in four lines. The messages had begun *Chela* until the year her mother left and *Graciela* ever after, and Graciela had never asked why, because a question took ninety-three hours to arrive and ninety-three to come back, and by then she would have had to mean it.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-1
upsertNodes.text:
The console was in the next module, with a second chair that was also a crate. Graciela laid her kit out on the deck in the order she would need it, which was the order she had packed it in, which was the only order she trusted. First the clock: she synchronized the station's to the *Starling*'s, found them four tenths of a second apart, logged the difference, and felt better. Then the pipeline.

"Single-window difference imaging," she said, because her mother was standing behind her and not asking. "Each time La Mancha comes round, it compares that one window with your static model and flags whatever changed. Mostly it's a fault detector: something drifts, it tells you before you'd see it."

"Before I'd see it," her mother said.

"Before anyone would."

"Is there someone?" her mother asked a while later, while the first calibration ran. "At home."

Graciela watched the progress bar. She thought about the question for the length of the calibration, which was four minutes, which was nothing, which was the fastest she had answered her mother in a decade.

"Tomás," she said. "He asked me not to come. When I came anyway he said he'd wait. Two years."

Her mother said nothing to that, and Graciela found she was grateful, and that she could not have said so in a letter either.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-2
upsertNodes.text:
She wrote the report the next day, the way she wrote everything that went to Earth: slowly, and more than once. First she tried to find a way for no one to be doing it. On Earth, on dry slopes, shrubs arranged themselves into bands like these with nobody cutting anything, water and roots working it out between them; tiger bush, the ecologists called it. But bands like that bent with the ground and forked, and no two of them kept quite the same pace. She went through all twelve. They ran straight, none of them forked, and every one had moved the same 3.1 kilometres, to a tenth of a pixel. *Linear parallel features in La Mancha, about eight kilometres wide, advancing east at 3.1 km per orbit in the planet-fixed frame; instrument origin excluded by reprojection across two windows; self-organised banding disfavoured (no curvature, no forks, a single rate). Interpretation: consistent with cultivation by an agent. A grazing front or a die-back front is not excluded.* She took out *consistent with* and put it back. She took out *by an agent* and put it back. She thought of a committee on Earth reading it in four days, and wrote it plainer.

At 14:20 on the tenth day she sent it, and it began its ninety-three hours. Any answer would reach the station on the eighteenth day. The *Starling* would leave on the sixteenth.

When she looked up the console module was empty. The crate had its cushion and its cord and no one on it. On the comms panel the *Starling*'s crew channel showed a message being composed, outbound, to Earth, a long one; the counter said it had been open for an hour and twelve minutes.

She had not heard her daughter leave.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
* * *

The window on the fourteenth came in at 06:05, and the edges had moved again: 3.1 kilometres, the same as before, as if whoever was doing it kept a calendar. Three windows now, one orbit apart, agreeing. Graciela ran the reprojection twice and logged it and did not tell her mother that she had run it twice.

On the fifteenth she crossed to the *Starling* at six in the morning, before her mother was up, and found Kaya in the cockpit doing the departure checklist with a bulb of coffee held in his teeth.

"I'm not coming," she said. "I wrote to the agency on the tenth; they've had it since yesterday. I'll sign whatever they need. The station needs someone in the loop; you've heard her, a question to Earth takes longer than an orbit. My mother's done eleven years. She goes home. I stay."

Kaya took the coffee out of his mouth. He looked at her for a long moment with an expression she could not read, and then he began, very quietly, to laugh.

"What."

"Your mother," Kaya said, "was here an hour ago." He wiped his eyes. "She's staying, and you're going home to your Tomás, and she'd take it as a kindness if I didn't let you argue."

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
Graciela stood in the cockpit door with her hand on the frame. She thought, with great clarity, of every message she had ever timed. She thought of her mother at five in the morning in this same doorway, choosing her words the way she chose them for the agency, and doing it first, so that by the time Graciela knew, it would already be arranged.

"She timed it," she said.

Kaya put the coffee back in his teeth. "I leave at noon tomorrow. You two work out which of you I'm taking. Or neither," he added. "But I'd like to know by dinner."

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
"You'll write," Graciela said. And then, because there were no ninety-three hours to hide in, and no one to arrange it for her, she said the rest.

"You wrote to me every day, mamá. I have all of them. I used to read them at night and I could hear you choosing the words. And I answered in four lines, four days later. I'm not going home to wait for your letters. I got so good at waiting that I did it to Tomás."

She had not known she was going to say the last thing until it was said.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
Her mother said nothing for a long time. Then she said, "The stores are fourteen hundred and sixty person-days."

"I know what the stores are."

"Two of us is two years. The next ship is four."

"Kaya can leave what he brought for us going home," Graciela said. "Six hundred and seventy."

"Nearly three years, then." Her mother did the division without looking up. "It's a bet. That they read the report and send a ship early. That they believe it."

"They'll believe it."

"We can't know that before noon tomorrow."

"No," Graciela said. "We can't know anything before noon tomorrow. That's what it's like here. You told me."

Graciela thought of her mother alone here for four more years, sixty-two, with the only thing like it anyone had ever seen and no one to tell in less than four days.

"A grazing front would do everything I've shown them," her mother said. "Showing them it isn't one is work for two."

Graciela waited.

"Both, then," her mother said.

"Both."

It was not what either of them had arranged. It was, Graciela thought, the first thing since she was eighteen that they had decided in the same room.

No whole-scene flag in any scene. Scene 3 now audits canon.request as well (narrated 0.92), and scene 2 withholds it from the reader, as the disclosure plan intends. Purpose, author-stated: a hard science-fiction story in which the first sign of other minds is a pattern that patience hid, and a mother and daughter who have loved each other only across a four-day delay learn to answer in real time; the drawn ending realized as their choice. Verdict: fulfilled, with one optional note. Evidence: the discovery now includes the step a careful observer takes before the word agent (s2-p6: she tries to find a way for no one to be doing it, checks the bands against tiger bush, and finds them straight, unforked and all at one rate), which serves the first purpose twice: patience hid the pattern, and procedure, not excitement, admits it. The report still leaves a grazing front open, so in s3-p5 believing it is a real question with a price: nearly three years of food against a ship in four. The ending is now their choice in their own words: Candelaria gives one reason aloud, in the report’s terms, and Graciela waits instead of arranging; the Send it now reversal and the finished sentence at the end carry the real-time answer. The two light clauses and the corrected rations make the physical world consistent without explanation. Optional, artistic rather than coherence: Tomas is still thin for the cost he carries; one concrete detail of his own in s1-p5 would give the letter in s3-p6 a person behind it. It found the tiger-bush passage to be exposition staged as argument. Soft spots, new: (1) eleven months to 672 AU averages about 3,500 km/s, over 1 percent of light speed, a torch ship the story never reckons with, odd beside stores counted to the person-day; (2) lens imaging needs long integration, so a single window resolving 8 km stripes asks for faith; (3) tiger bush is the weaker foil: wind-driven fir waves are parallel, evenly spaced and advance together downwind, the obvious non-agent explanation on a tidally locked world with a permanent wind, which the rule-out as written would not exclude. Craft: 'I didn't know it a week ago' narrates the mother's arc; echoes remain audible; Kaya's 'Or neither' hands the women their answer; the cost is on the page as arithmetic but never as fear, and nobody notices that staying short of food forces Earth's hand, the move they have just stopped making on each other; weakest lines: 'She had not known she was going to say the last thing until it was said', 'an expression she could not read', and the tense knot in 'it will have been true for a whole day that you could still have gone'; after 'Then the arithmetic came' the next 'she' briefly reads as Graciela. upsertNodes.text: The Starling is a fusion torch that crosses the 672 AU in eleven months, about 1.2 percent of light speed on average, on a fixed propellant plan; it must leave the Landing by day 16 to reach Earth on that plan and its consumables, and it cannot wait. The agency can afford one such flight about every four years.

The autonomy installation includes a new single-window difference-imaging pipeline with a fault detector: it compares each observing window with the station's accumulated static model and flags what has changed. One window is far too noisy to make a map from, but not too noisy to disagree with the eleven-year static model, so the pipeline can see change that a single window could never map.

TRAPPIST-1e is tidally locked to its red dwarf, with a permanent circulation whose surface wind blows east across La Mancha, and the light arriving at the Landing left it 40.7 years ago. La Mancha is a dark region about 900 km across on its eastern terminator, named by Candelaria as a joke on stain and on the wheat plain of La Mancha; since 2226 it has been known to be a photosynthetic mat, black across the visible and near infrared.

On day 10 Candelaria sends the agency a hedged report of straight parallel swaths advancing across La Mancha, with the frame test. Before sending it she rules out self-organised banding by water of the kind tiger bush makes on Earth: the swaths are straight, never fork, and all advance at one rate. She cannot rule out a wind-driven die-back wave of the kind fir waves make on Earth, which would be straight, parallel and in step moving downwind, and the report names it, with a grazing front, as not excluded. It reaches Earth about day 13.9; no reply can arrive before the Starling must leave.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-1
upsertNodes.text:
The docking tube was forty metres of ribbed white fabric, and the Sun was in it.

It came through a port halfway along, a point so bright that Graciela put up her hand without thinking, and in the unlit tube her hand threw a shadow on the wall with edges as clean as a cut. She had read that it would be like this: at six hundred and seventy-two astronomical units the Sun was three seconds of arc across, which is to say a point, and about as bright as a full Moon over Valparaíso. Reading it had not prepared her for the shadow. Nothing in eleven months on the *Starling* had cast one.

Behind her Kaya, who with Brandt made up the *Starling*'s entire crew, said, "Sixteen days," the way he had said it every morning of the approach, as if it were a greeting. The return burn was fixed: the *Starling* was a fusion torch, it had averaged a hundredth of the speed of light to get here, and a torch kept to its propellant plan or did not get home. On the sixteenth day the ship would leave, with the autonomy installed or not, and with the station's resident aboard.

"I know," she said, and pulled herself on.

Through the next port there was nothing to see, which was correct. Twelve one-metre telescopes held formation out there across a patch of dark three kilometres wide, the image plane, where the Sun's gravity brought one planet's light to a focus. They flew with their lights off, so as not to see themselves.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-1
upsertNodes.text:
The console was in the next module, with a second chair that was also a crate. Graciela laid her kit out on the deck in the order she would need it, which was the order she had packed it in, which was the only order she trusted. First the clock: she synchronized the station's to the *Starling*'s, found them four tenths of a second apart, logged the difference, and felt better. Then the pipeline.

"Single-window difference imaging," she said, because her mother was standing behind her and not asking. "Each time La Mancha comes round, it compares that one window with your static model and flags whatever changed. One window is far too noisy to make a map from. It isn't too noisy to disagree with one. Mostly it's a fault detector: something drifts, it tells you before you'd see it."

"Before I'd see it," her mother said.

"Before anyone would."

"Is there someone?" her mother asked a while later, while the first calibration ran. "At home."

Graciela watched the progress bar. She thought about the question for the length of the calibration, which was four minutes, which was nothing, which was the fastest she had answered her mother in a decade.

"Tomás," she said. "He asked me not to come. When I came anyway he said he'd wait. Two years."

Her mother said nothing to that, and Graciela found she was grateful, and that she could not have said so in a letter either.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-2
upsertNodes.text:
Then the arithmetic came, because it always came. A dozen swaths, eight kilometres wide and seventy-five apart, were moving east together, so any one place was cut again every five months, just as it had grown back; in the years Candelaria had been watching, every part of La Mancha had been cut twenty-seven times. Her change checks had been built for clouds, at forty kilometres a pixel, where an eight-kilometre swath is not there at all.

She had integrated it away. The patience she was best at had kept for her, faithfully, the average of all that cutting: the even dark on her map. The field had never once held still.

She found that she was standing in the galley with the kettle in her hand, and did not remember going there. She thought about the ones who cut. She thought about light that had left forty years ago, about whatever had done this before her daughter was born, which might have stopped since or might be doing it tonight, in a present she would never see. She thought about 2220, her first month here, and how she had decided then that the field was quiet. She did not, she noticed later, think about her daughter at all.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-2
upsertNodes.text:
She wrote the report the next day, the way she wrote everything that went to Earth: slowly, and more than once. First she tried to find a way for no one to be doing it. On Earth, on dry slopes, shrubs arranged themselves into bands like these with nobody cutting anything, water and roots working it out between them; tiger bush, the ecologists called it. But bands like that bent with the ground and forked, and no two of them kept quite the same pace. She went through all twelve. They ran straight, none of them forked, and every one had moved the same 3.1 kilometres, to a tenth of a pixel. The fir waves were harder. On windy mountainsides whole bands of fir died on the side facing the wind while seedlings came up behind them, so the bands walked downwind, straight and in step; nothing on TRAPPIST-1e was steadier than its wind, and nothing said how fast such a wave would walk under a red sun. That one she could not take back from here. *Linear parallel features in La Mancha, about eight kilometres wide, advancing east at 3.1 km per orbit in the planet-fixed frame; instrument origin excluded by reprojection across two windows; self-organised banding by water disfavoured (no curvature, no forks, a single rate). Interpretation: consistent with cultivation by an agent. A grazing front, or a wind-driven die-back wave of the fir-wave kind, is not excluded.* She took out *consistent with* and put it back. She took out *by an agent* and put it back. She thought of a committee on Earth reading it in four days, and wrote it plainer.

At 14:20 on the tenth day she sent it, and it began its ninety-three hours. Any answer would reach the station on the eighteenth day. The *Starling* would leave on the sixteenth.

When she looked up the console module was empty. The crate had its cushion and its cord and no one on it. On the comms panel the *Starling*'s crew channel showed a message being composed, outbound, to Earth, a long one; the counter said it had been open for an hour and twelve minutes.

She had not heard her daughter leave.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
* * *

The window on the fourteenth came in at 06:05, and the edges had moved again: 3.1 kilometres, the same as before, as if whoever was doing it kept a calendar. Three windows now, one orbit apart, agreeing. Graciela ran the reprojection twice and logged it and did not tell her mother that she had run it twice.

On the fifteenth she crossed to the *Starling* at six in the morning, before her mother was up, and found Kaya in the cockpit doing the departure checklist with a bulb of coffee held in his teeth.

"I'm not coming," she said. "I wrote to the agency on the tenth; they've had it since yesterday. I'll sign whatever they need. The station needs someone in the loop; you've heard her, a question to Earth takes longer than an orbit. My mother's done eleven years. She goes home. I stay."

Kaya took the coffee out of his mouth. He looked at her for a long moment, and then he began, very quietly, to laugh.

"What."

"Your mother," Kaya said, "was here an hour ago." He wiped his eyes. "She's staying, and you're going home to your Tomás, and she'd take it as a kindness if I didn't let you argue."

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
Graciela stood in the cockpit door with her hand on the frame. She thought, with great clarity, of every message she had ever timed. She thought of her mother at five in the morning in this same doorway, choosing her words the way she chose them for the agency, and doing it first, so that by the time Graciela knew, it would already be arranged.

"She timed it," she said.

Kaya put the coffee back in his teeth. "I leave at noon tomorrow. You two work out which of you I'm taking. I'd like to know by dinner."

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
Her mother was in the galley, in the one chair, with two mugs on the counter. She had not drunk from either.

"Kaya told you," she said.

"Kaya told me."

"Chela—" Her mother stopped, and this time did not correct it. "Tomás said two years. You told me that the first night. Two years is— he's waiting now, today. That doesn't keep." She turned one of the mugs a quarter turn. "You go home. I'll write. I'll write every day, I've had the practice."

It was the most she had said at once since the arrival, and none of it was in order, and Graciela understood that her mother had not rehearsed it, or had rehearsed it and lost the order on the way.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
"You'll write," Graciela said. And then, because there were no ninety-three hours to hide in, and no one to arrange it for her, she said the rest.

"You wrote to me every day, mamá. I have all of them. I used to read them at night and I could hear you choosing the words. And I answered in four lines, four days later. I'm not going home to wait for your letters. I got so good at waiting that I did it to Tomás."

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
Her mother said nothing for a long time. Then she said, "The stores are fourteen hundred and sixty person-days."

"I know what the stores are."

"Two of us is two years. The next ship is four."

"Kaya can leave what he brought for us going home," Graciela said. "Six hundred and seventy."

"Nearly three years, then." Her mother did the division without looking up. "It's a bet. That they read the report and send a ship early. That they believe it."

"They'll believe it."

"We can't know that before noon tomorrow."

"No," Graciela said. "We can't know anything before noon tomorrow. That's what it's like here. You told me."

Graciela thought of her mother alone here for four more years, sixty-two, with the only thing like it anyone had ever seen and no one to tell in less than four days.

"A wind wave would do everything I've shown them," her mother said. "Showing them it isn't one is work for two."

Graciela waited.

"Both, then," her mother said.

"Both."

It was not what either of them had arranged. It was, Graciela thought, the first thing since she was eighteen that they had decided in the same room.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
She wrote to Tomás in the console module, on the crate. It took an hour and it was not four lines. It ended with the date of the next ship and one sentence she rewrote six times: *I am asking you to wait, which is the thing I never forgave anyone for asking.* When it was done she set the send time for 12:05 tomorrow, five minutes after the *Starling* would be gone, and looked at that for a while.

"Send it now," her mother said from the door.

"He can't answer in time. It gets there after the ship's gone either way."

"That isn't what it's for." Her mother did not come in. "Send it now, and it leaves while you could still change your mind. He should have that."

Graciela thought about a message that had arrived when *don't* was a word about the past. She cleared the send time, and sent it, and it began its ninety-three hours to Valparaíso.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
At noon on the sixteenth Kaya and Brandt took the *Starling* off the collar. They watched from the galley port. For a few minutes it was a shape, its drive not yet lit, and then the drive lit and it was a point, and then it was a point that moved, which was the only way to tell it from a star.

When it was gone Graciela did the division again, although she knew the answer. Food for nearly three years; the next ship in four.

upsertNodes.subject: scene-3
upsertNodes.text:
Afterwards her mother took the one chair and Graciela took the crate, and they began on the next window, which was four days out. "If we put seven and nine in the near infrared," her mother said, "a dying edge should come up as a slope, and a cut one—"

"—as a step, by the second pass," Graciela said. "I've already queued it."

Her mother looked at her. On the counter between them the Sun lay in its spot the size of a lentil, and neither of them said anything about how long the answer had taken.

upsertNodes.text:
The docking tube was forty metres of ribbed white fabric, and the Sun was in it.

It came through a port halfway along, a point so bright that Graciela put up her hand without thinking, and in the unlit tube her hand threw a shadow on the wall with edges as clean as a cut. She had read that it would be like this: at six hundred and seventy-two astronomical units the Sun was three seconds of arc across, which is to say a point, and about as bright as a full Moon over Valparaíso. Reading it had not prepared her for the shadow. Nothing in eleven months on the *Starling* had cast one.

Behind her Kaya, who with Brandt made up the *Starling*'s entire crew, said, "Sixteen days," the way he had said it every morning of the approach, as if it were a greeting. The return burn was fixed: the *Starling* was a fusion torch, it had averaged more than a hundredth of the speed of light to get here, and a torch kept to its propellant plan or did not get home. On the sixteenth day the ship would leave, with the autonomy installed or not, and with the station's resident aboard.

"I know," she said, and pulled herself on.

Through the next port there was nothing to see, which was correct. Twelve one-metre telescopes held formation out there across a patch of dark three kilometres wide, the image plane, where the Sun's gravity brought one planet's light to a focus. They flew with their lights off, so as not to see themselves.

upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Whole-work purpose review of version 4 (self-review by the calling LLM, after deepening pass 3; independent readings are independent-reader-1, -2 and -3). Purpose, author-stated, unchanged. Verdict: fulfilled. Evidence beyond version 3: the discovery now meets its strongest natural rival honestly. Candelaria rules out banding by water and cannot rule out a wind wave, so the report stays hedged for a reason the reader can check, and the ending turns that hedge into work: the near-infrared pass that would show a cut step or a dying slope is what the two of them start on, so the last scene’s collaboration is also the first move in the bet. The torch clause makes the fixed burn and the rationed stores one economy. The last scene is quieter: Kaya no longer offers the answer, the mother’s arc is not narrated, and the fear of the bet appears once, in character. Risks: scene 2 carries more exposition than before (tiger bush, fir waves), and the fir-wave sentences are the densest science prose in the story; Tomas is still thin. No further revision suggested in this session.","data":{"taskHash":"5aadedbc7568ae29b5c990569817f1f9e5320d549dfc29cb42881b42d30fbf44","unit":"whole_work","verdict":"fulfilled","words":3607,"textSha256":"6d04e6dcd06d27240bbd03b8f90fe8dbf43c163326aad9c81698913d6118722b","projectionHash":"0d7aea49b4c1af50e242c8b856264f3f5bf807fc7a8c55c185e31e5a7f31e2fa","advisory":["scene-2 exposition density (tiger bush and fir waves)","Tomas thin"],"reviewer":"self-review"},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":105}}

upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Voice review of the passages changed in deepening pass 3 (self-review). (1) Graciela, s1-p5: \"One window is far too noisy to make a map from. It isn’t too noisy to disagree with one.\" Two short declaratives in her engineer’s register, the same register as \"Mostly it’s a fault detector\"; it explains the pipeline to her mother without condescension. Keep. (2) Candelaria, s2-p6: the fir-wave sentences keep her method (take the word back first; say what she cannot exclude), and \"That one she could not take back from here\" is her own measure of honesty. Risk: with tiger bush before it, this is the densest science in the story. (3) Candelaria, s3-p5: \"A wind wave would do everything I’ve shown them\" now names the rival in her report’s terms. Keep. (4) Candelaria, s3-p3: without the narrated arc, \"That doesn’t keep\" stands alone, which is how she speaks. (5) Graciela, s3-p7: doing the division again although she knows the answer is her checking habit (she ran the reprojection twice and did not say so), used for fear. (6) Both, s3-p8: the finished sentence is now the test itself, a dying slope against a cut step, so the echo carries the plot. (7) Author: the torch clause in s1-p1 keeps d.procedure’s preference for stated constraints over description.","data":{"modelHash":"23dd5f6392ec1d1b9720e90ce2626f6f36733252b98f1c6d31ca59ecc75713e0","authorModelNodeId":"author-model","subjects":{"author":["d.procedure"],"referent.astronomer":["cut.astronomer.d10.interpretation","cut.astronomer.reliance.d15"],"referent.engineer":["life-trends#tr.control"]},"risk":"scene-2 exposition density"},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":106}}

upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Fourth independent fresh-context reading, of version 4 (text 6d04e6dc): a Claude subagent that received only export/integration-time.md, with no model, graph, notes or earlier reports; independent of this run's context, not of the model family. Verdict: \"I'd buy it after a light rewrite\": the science is unusually well worked and the discovery scene turns it into drama, but the ending needs one less echo and one real cost. It checked and found holding nearly every number, including 0.0116c for the voyage, 670 person-days as two passengers for 335 days, the Einstein ring at 1.1 solar radii, and the window times; tiger bush and fir waves are right and the report hedges honestly. Three things wobble: (1) at forty kilometres a pixel an eight-kilometre swath is diluted to a fifth, not erased, so 'not there at all' overstates; say the cloud checks compared orbit to orbit or had a high threshold; (2) the torch is lit minutes after undocking and watched through the Sun-facing port, so its exhaust would point at them and it would not pass for a star; (3) the famine bet dissolves at the next division: 2,130 person-days for two over four years is three-quarter rations, which these two would see at once. Craft: Kaya's laugh does the reader's recognizing; the report's italics restate the paragraph before them; 'could not take back from here' should be 'could not rule out'; 'I got so good at waiting that I did it to Tomás' slides from waiting to making someone wait; the closing repeats the symmetry (decided in the same room, the finished sentences, the play on the answer). Asks: halve the report paragraph; put the cost in the body by having Candelaria do the second division aloud, and cut Kaya's laugh.","data":{"reviewer":"fresh-context Claude subagent (general-purpose), read only export/integration-time.md (v4)","verdict":"buy after a light rewrite","physicsErrors":["40 km pixels dilute an 8 km swath to a fifth, not to nothing","a torch lit minutes after undocking points its exhaust at the station and would not pass for a star","2,130 person-days for two over four years is three-quarter rations, not famine"],"craft":["Kaya's laugh does the recognizing","report italics restate the narration","'could not take back' should be 'could not rule out'","the Tomas line slides from waiting to making someone wait","one closing echo too many"],"asks":["halve the report paragraph","Candelaria does the second division aloud; cut Kaya's laugh"],"report":"notes/06-fourth-reader.md"},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":107}}

Self-review compared with independent reading (independent-reader-4 read version 4 blind). upsertNodes.text: The Starling is a fusion torch that crosses the 672 AU in eleven months, about 1.2 percent of light speed on average, on a fixed propellant plan; it lights its drive only when well clear of the station, and it must leave the Landing by day 16 to reach Earth on that plan and its consumables, and it cannot wait. The agency can afford one such flight about every four years.

On day 15 both women decide to stay at the Landing. The Starling will leave on day 16 with its two-person crew and leave behind the rations it carried for them; two residents then have nearly three years of stores against a relief ship about four years away: four years on about three-quarter rations unless a ship comes early.

The station's stores hold 1,460 person-days: one resident for four years, two for about two. The Starling carries about 670 person-days for its two returning passengers on the eleven-month voyage home and can leave them, which gives two residents nearly three years in all, or four years on about three-quarter rations. The next scheduled relief ship is about four years away.

A dozen swaths, each about 8 km wide and about 75 km from the next, all advance east 3.1 km per orbit, so any one place is cut again about every 148 days, and the mat regrows over a swath in about 145 days: a rotation, not a single front. Over eleven years every part of La Mancha was cut and regrew some twenty-seven times, and the long average is uniform. The station's own change checks were for clouds: they compared each orbit with the last at about 40 km per pixel, where a swath that has moved on 3.1 km, cut at one edge and regrowing behind, changes a pixel less than a thin cloud would. The 3.1 km shift is measured by fitting each swath edge to a fraction of a 3.8 km pixel against the static model.
